## An acquired right isn't a blank cheque

The phrase comes up often during a visit or in a listing: "there are acquired rights on this lot." It's sometimes used as if it settles every question about what can be done with land in the agricultural zone. In reality, an acquired right is far narrower than the phrase suggests — and knowing exactly what it covers avoids unpleasant surprises after the purchase. It's a distinct question from the [14 criteria the CPTAQ applies](../cptaq-zone-agricole/index.qmd) to approve a non-agricultural use in the green zone.

## What an acquired right actually protects

An acquired right recognizes a non-agricultural use or building that already existed before agricultural zoning, or a specific CPTAQ decision, came to regulate it. It protects that exact use, in its exact form, at that specific location — not a general right to do whatever one wants with the lot afterward. Two neighbouring lots can have entirely different histories, and therefore acquired rights that look nothing alike.

## What it doesn't cover

Expanding an existing building, switching to a different non-agricultural use, or resuming an activity after a long interruption are generally not covered by the original acquired right. These situations most often require a separate application to the CPTAQ, even if the initial use was perfectly legitimate. An acquired right doesn't grow over time, and it doesn't expand with a change of owner.

## What gets verified, not assumed

An acquired right isn't automatically passed on "on trust" to a new buyer: its validity rests on proof of continuous use, often documented through historical aerial photos, permits, or successive municipal assessments. Before treating a use as acquired, it's worth asking the seller or notary what evidence actually exists, rather than relying on a claim passed down from one owner to the next for decades.

## A nuance that changes an offer

A buyer who plans to maintain, expand, or resume a particular use on agricultural land benefits from understanding this distinction before signing, not after. What the law protects is precise. What local use and habit suggest is sometimes a good deal looser.
